KEY CHALLENGES Identifying correct service boundaries Avoiding circular dependencies Avoiding overly large services Sync vs async communication decisions Avoiding overly small services / nanoservices Defining ownership of functionality Managing cross-cutting concerns Defining bounded contexts Versioning service contracts Managing service dependencies Preventing a distributed monolith Classic failure : Order → Payment → Inventory → User → Shipping, all called synchronously per request. That's not microservices. It's a distributed monolith with extra network hops.

02 Communication A method call becomes a network call. MONOLITH MICROSERVICES KEY CHALLENGES Network latency (1 ms → 5–100+ ms) Partial failures & packet loss Network & connection failures Retries and duplicate requests DNS failures Serialization / deserialization cost Connection pool exhaustion API compatibility across services Socket / read / write timeouts What used to be a 1 ms in-process call can now fail independently of the caller. This is the single biggest mindset shift when moving to microservices.

03 Resilience One service goes down. The rest must survive. E v e ry r e mot e c a ll n eed s a n e xp lici t f a il ur e str a t eg y KEY CHALLENGES Timeouts on every remote call Fallback responses Retry policies (with backoff) Backpressure Circuit breakers Load shedding Bulkheads (failure isolation) Graceful degradation Rate limiting In a monolith, A → B → C usually fails together as one process. In microservices, B can be down while A keeps running, so every downstream call needs an explicit failure strategy.

KEY CHALLENGES Centralized logging (ELK / OpenSearch) Correlation ID propagation Metrics (Prometheus / Grafana) Trace ID / Span ID propagation Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry, Jaeger / Tempo) API contracts, versioning & gateway auth also live here A single business request can generate hundreds of log lines across many services.
